t: Minimum Operations to Sort a String — Descending Runs
o: Each operation sorts a proper (non-full) substring. 'dog' needs 1 (sort 'og'), 'card' needs 2 ('ca' region and 'rd' region), 'gf' is impossible. The structural driver is adjacent inversions: a position i with s[i] > s[i+1] is a 'break' that must be repaired by an operation whose interval covers it, and one operation repairs exactly one maximal descending run. If the entire string is one descending run, the only operation that could repair the final break is sorting the whole string — forbidden — so the answer is -1.
k: Every adjacent descent s[i] > s[i+1] requires an operation covering that boundary.
One operation fixes exactly one maximal descending run (sorting it makes that segment non-decreasing).
Already-sorted strings cost 0; a fully descending string is unsolvable because the needed operation would be the whole string.

a.i: Scan adjacent pairs; the answer is the number of descents, with special cases for sorted (0) and fully descending (-1).
s: If n == 2 and s is unsorted, return -1 (any repair needs the whole string).
If s is strictly decreasing, return -1.
Otherwise return the count of indices with s[i] > s[i+1].
a.t: O(n) — a couple of linear scans

w: The linear scan is the way to go. Common pitfalls: forgetting the -1 cases (fully descending strings, and length-2 unsorted strings where no proper substring of length ≥ 2 exists), and treating equal adjacent characters as descents (they are not). Follow-ups: what if sorting the whole string were allowed (then the answer is 1 whenever unsorted)? What if only reversals were allowed?
